13: 1st 1775-82: factionalism, Surat 1775 to Salbai 1782. 2nd 1803-05: factionalism, Bassein 1802, Marathas lost. 3rd 1817-19: EIC breached the SA, Marathas lost, Swarajya annexed.
The EIC needed the Deccan: long coastline, Gujarat-China cotton trade, Maratha hold on parts of the Malabar coast. The Marathas and Mysore were the last powers able to check it.
Raghunath Rao 73-74 was removed in 1774 by Nana Fadnis (Baarbhai). He turned to Bombay's Hornby and signed Surat 1775: EIC help for Salsette, Bassein and revenue.
Warren Hastings 73-85 cancelled Surat to save cost; Purandhar 1776 with Nana Fadnis recognised Madhav Rao II 74-95. Bombay kept sheltering Raghunath, Nana offered the French a port, war resumed.
Wadgaon 1779: Nana Fadnis, Mahadji Scindhia and Tukoji Rao Holkar beat the EIC. Both tired, so Mahadji signed Salbai 1782 at Gwalior: territory returned, no French, Madhav Rao II 74-95 recognised.
Salbai 1782 to Bassein 1802 was decline: Mahadji died 1794, Madhav Rao II 74-95 suicide 1795, Bajirao II 96-18 Peshwa 1796, Nana Fadnis died 1800. Wellesley 98-05 was waiting.
Bajirao II 96-18 had Vithoji Rao Holkar executed in 1801. To avenge him, Yashwantrao Holkar beat the Peshwa and Scindhia. Bajirao fled and signed Bassein (Dec 1802), an SA ending the Svarajya army.
The SA united old rivals: Scindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle fought. Arthur Wellesley at Assaye 1803: toughest fight. Marathas lost; Scindhia lost Delhi, Agra, Gujarat. Wellesley 98-05 recalled for the cost.

The EIC paused after Wellesley 98-05, and Pindaris raided. Francis Hastings 13-23 crushed them and began Paramountcy 1813-58. Appa Sahib signed an SA in 1816 but used its loophole to hire mercenaries.
Bajirao II 96-18, Appa Sahib and Yashwantrao Holkar rose in 1817. Appa lost at Sitabuldi, Holkar at Mahidpur; Koregaon 1 January 1818 held. About 1.2 lakh EIC troops; Bajirao surrendered June 1818.

Peshwaship abolished; Bajirao II 96-18 pensioned to Bithur, where his son Nana Sahib later led Kanpur 1857. Svarajya joined Bombay Presidency. Appa Sahib deposed. Satara and Kolhapur spared; Satara annexed 1848.

Four reasons: factionalism, no unified command, EIC finances, EIC naval and logistics edge. The EIC army then overhyped border threats: Nepal 1814-16, Burma 1824-26, Afghanistan 1838-42, Sindh 1843, Sikh wars.
14: In 1600 the EIC came to trade, not rule, and its army was small. It interfered only when it gained, as after Buxar 1764. After 1757 its interference kept rising.
Francis Hastings 13-23 began Paramountcy in 1813: the Company State is supreme, British interests first, annex if needed. It was the Subsidiary Alliance minus the rights of the Indian State.
Dalhousie 48-56 used Paramountcy three ways: Lapse, wars (Punjab 1849, Pegu 1852-53), annexation in lieu of subsidy (Berar 1853). By 1856 the Company State held 63% of land and 78% of people.

Court of Directors formulated Lapse in 1847; Dalhousie 48-56 applied it: no biological heir, rights lapse. Seven States fell 1848-54; Inam Commission 1852 seized estates; Nana Sahib's pension was refused.
Hyderabad could not pay its subsidy, so Dalhousie 48-56 annexed Berar in 1853. Awadh followed a chain from 1765; the rest was taken in 1856 for maladministration, not Lapse.
Ranjit Singh 01-39 kept the Sikh State a strong friendly buffer; after 1839 four factions tore it apart. Lahore 1846 cut the army, Amritsar 1846 sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh.
Mulraj and Chattar Singh revolted in 1848, giving Dalhousie 48-56 his chance. Punjab was annexed in 1849 from child Duleep Singh 43-49; the Koh-i-Noor went to the Crown.
The 2nd Anglo-Burmese War 1852-53 annexed Pegu; with Arakan and Tenasserim the Bay of Bengal became a British lake. The Arabian Sea coast fell from Bombay 1668 to Sindh 1843.
Dalhousie 48-56 also built modern India: railways from 1853, telegraph, Post Office Act 1854, PWD, GT Road, Wood's Despatch 1854. Motives: troops, cheaper rule, raw materials, markets.
Each policy built on the last, so 1857 came when it did. Dalhousie 48-56 won land but lost legitimacy: Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Sahib, Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57, Awadh court, Sikh soldiers aggrieved.
Canning 56-62 inherited the revolt. Government of India Act 1858 ended the Company State; Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858 ended Lapse and respected rulers' rights. No more annexations.
15: Britain was proud: first modern democracy, Industrial Revolution, Seven Years' Global War victory, Napoleon beaten, science and capitalism. It felt destined to lead and civilise: the White Man's Burden.
Before 1813 the EIC was scared, and William Jones found Sanskrit older than Greek and Latin. So Orientalism: rule India the India way, with its laws and languages. Warren Hastings 73-85 led.

Four institutions: Calcutta Madrasa 1781 (Warren Hastings 73-85), Asiatic Society 1784 (Sir William Jones), Sanskrit College Banaras 1791 (Jonathan Duncan), Fort William College 1800 (Wellesley 98-05).
Critics said India's past was glorious but its present degenerate. So Cornwallis 86-93 ruled the English way: British senior posts, Collector not Judge, Permanent Settlement 1793, an Aloof Elite.
Thomas Munro, Madras 1820-27, used Indian forms but kept all power with the EIC: Orientalist in form, Authoritarian in substance. His Ryotwari had EIC officials collect everything.

By 1813 the army was huge, Napoleon beaten, a market waiting. Three ideas filled the space: Liberalism (Macaulay), Utilitarianism (Bentham, James Mill), Evangelicalism (Charles Grant, Charter Act 1813).
Bentinck 28-35 to Macaulay's Minute 1835 was Liberal confidence at its peak: Sati Abolition Act 1829, Thuggee suppression under Captain Sleeman, English replacing Persian, uniform criminal procedure.
The Revolt of 1857 shook the British and broke the paternalistic story. Reform retreated, race hardened, Authoritarianism rose. Lytton 76-80 and Curzon 99-05 were its architects.

Fearing Russia, the British pushed into Afghanistan: Auckland 36-42's war 1839-42, Lytton 76-80's war 1878-80 and Gandamak 1879, then Ripon 80-84's reversal. The 1907 Convention ended the Persian flank.
Dufferin 84-88 annexed Upper Burma in January 1886, deposing King Thibaw, the last major extension. Imperial Preference, formalised at Ottawa 1932, gave British goods lower tariffs.
The burden produced its opposite: American and French Revolutions, 1830 and 1848, the Irish struggle. Ideas travelled through Gandhi from South Africa and Nehru from Cambridge.
